Once this identification has been made, we can evaluate amplitudes using multi-loop techniques, that will be described in the next chapter.

Chapter 3
Multi-loop techniques in Quantum Field Theory

In the previous chapter we saw that within the Effective Field Theory of General Relativity, near-zone computations involve multi-loop two-point functions whereas far-zone computations require the evaluation of multi-loop one-point functions.
These Feynman integrals are difficult to compute in general, and we need to develop a systematic procedure to make efficient computations.
The evaluation of each Feynman Integral in general can be very time-consuming, therefore each identity which relate different integrals, can greatly simplify the problem of their determination and consequently the calculation of loop corrections as a whole.

The general procedure that one adopts is to use the several relations among the different integrals to decompose them in a minimal set of integrals, known as Master Integrals (MI), which constitute a basis. To do that we will follow a three-step procedure, which will be described in the following sections, which are:

1.

Tensor decomposition: in which we decompose the tensorial structure of the amplitude in terms of a linear combination of independent Lorentz vectors and Tensor, multiplied by some coefficients known as
form factors
.

2.

Reduction to Master Integrals (MI): in which we will use the powerful identities relating the different Feynman integrals, such as the
integration-by-parts
(IBP) identities
[
55
,
56
]
, to decompose the form factors in a basis of integrals, which are the Master Integrals.

3.

Master Integral evaluation: in which we will evaluate the Master Integrals appearing. This procedure can be done directly or using other methods such as
difference

[
57
,
58
]
or
differential equations
(DEs)
[
59
,
60
]
(for reviews see
[
61
,
62
]
).

Chapter organization

The chapter will be divided as follows:

•

We describe how to tensor decompose a generic amplitude in terms of Lorentz tensor multiplied by form factors, which can be obtained by means of projectors. We will then show how to compute the projectors that will be necessary for future calculations.

•

Then, we describe a general classification of multi-loop Feynman integrals, and how they are organized in topologies.

•

Furthermore, we will describe the symmetry relations among the various Feynman integrals, and how they can be used to decompose them in a basis of Master Integrals.

•

Eventually, we will directly compute some master integrals and scalar integrals that will be used in the following chapters.

3.1
Tensor Decomposition

The first step to take when one is dealing with a generic Feynman diagrams is to separate Lorentz and Dirac structures from the integrals, and an efficient way to do that is by using the so-called
tensor decomposition
. Let us consider a generic amplitude
\mathcal{M}
, where we expose all external polarization vectors as:

\mathcal{M}=\epsilon_{1}^{\mu_{1}}\cdots\epsilon_{k}^{\mu_{k}}\mathcal{M}_{\mu_{1}\cdots\mu_{k}}\ .

(3.1)

We can write an ansatz for the tensor
\mathcal{M}_{\mu_{1}\cdots\mu_{k}}
in terms of independent Lorentz vectors and tensors, and of the possible Dirac structures:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\mu_{1}\cdots\mu_{k}}=\sum_{i}f_{i}T_{\mu_{1}\cdots\mu_{k},i}

(3.2)

where
f_{i}
are called
form factors
.
The form factors
f_{i}
can be computed by
projections
, namely they can be extracted from the diagrams by the action of suitably chosen projectors
P_{i}
,

f_{i}=P_{i}\mathcal{M}\ .

(3.3)

Through the tensor decomposition, the numerators of the Feynman integrals appearing in the form factors
f_{i}
may include only scalar products build from the external momenta and the loop momenta.

An efficient way to find the projectors
P_{i}
is to use an ansatz of the same form of the one used for the tensor
\mathcal{M}_{\mu_{1}\cdots\mu_{k}}
:

P_{i}=\sum_{j}C_{ij}T_{j}\ ,

(3.4)

and to fix the coefficients by solving the following system of equations:

\displaystyle\begin{cases}P_{i}\cdot T_{j}=0\qquad ifi\neq j\\
P_{i}T_{i}=1\end{cases}\,.

(3.5)

3.1.1
Example: One-loop vacuum diagrams

Let us discuss an example which will be useful in the evaluations of PN corrections, which is the tensor decomposition of one-loop vacuum diagrams of the form:

\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{k^{i}k^{j};k^{i}k^{j}k^{k}k^{l};k^{i}k^{j}k^{k}k^{l}k^{m}k^{n}}{\mathbf{k}^{2}-k_{0}^{2}}

(3.6)

Notice that in this case we are integrating over the
d
spatial dimensions, whereas the energy component is treated as an effective mass term.
Since there are no external momenta involved in this process, these integrals can be tensor decomposed only as linear combinations of products of metric tensors. In the next chapter we will deal with tensor integrals of this type with at most 6 free indices, and so we will describe the tensor decomposition needed for these cases.

2-indices tensor decomposition

Let us consider a 1-loop integral with 2 free indices:

\displaystyle I_{2}^{ij}=\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{k^{i}k^{j}}{\mathbf{k}^{2}-k_{0}^{2}}

(3.7)

It has only two free indices, and so it must be proportional to the spatial metric
\delta^{ij}
as:

\displaystyle I_{2}^{ij}=A\delta^{ij}

(3.8)

In order to get the form factor
A
we can contract the integral
I_{2}^{ij}
with an appropriate projector
P_{A}^{ij}
such that:

\displaystyle A=I_{2}^{ij}P_{A\ ij}

(3.9)

We can write an ansatz for
P_{A}
and write it in terms of the Lorentz tensor appearing on RHS of eq.(
3.8
) as:

\displaystyle P_{A}^{ij}=C_{A}\delta^{ij}

(3.10)

and we can fix the coefficient
C_{A}
by solving the following equation:

\displaystyle P_{A}^{ij}\delta_{ij}=1,

(3.11)

which is solved for
C_{A}=\frac{1}{d}
, and so the projector is:

\displaystyle P_{A}^{ij}=\frac{1}{d}\delta^{ij},

(3.12)

and the form factor can be obtained as:

\displaystyle A=I_{2}^{ij}\frac{\delta_{ij}}{d}\ .

(3.13)

This simple prescription can be generalized for tensors involving more indices.

4-indices tensor decomposition

Consider the following 1-loop integral with 4 free Lorenz indices:

\displaystyle I_{4}^{ijkl}=\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{k^{i}k^{j}k^{k}k^{l}}{\mathbf{k}^{2}-k_{0}^{2}}

(3.14)

It can be written in terms of form factors as:

\displaystyle I_{4}^{ijkl}=A\delta^{ij}\delta^{kl}+B\delta^{ik}\delta^{jl}+C\delta^{il}\delta^{jk}

(3.15)

As in the previous case, we want to obtain form factors by contracting
I_{4}^{ijkl}
with appropriate projectors that have the following ansatz:

\displaystyle P^{ijkl}_{a}=C_{1\ a}\delta^{ij}\delta^{kl}+C_{2\ a}\delta^{ik}\delta^{jl}+C_{3\ a}\delta^{il}\delta^{jk}\qquad with\ a=A,B,C

(3.16)

where the coefficients can be fixed by solving the following system of equations:

\displaystyle P_{a}^{ijkl}g_{V\ ijkl}=V_{a}

(3.17)

where
g_{V\ ijkl}=(\delta^{ij}\delta^{kl},\delta^{ik}\delta^{jl},\delta^{il}\delta^{jk})^{T}
and
V_{a}
is a unit vector with values 1 in the
a
position and
0
in the rest.

6-indices tensor decomposition

Consider the following 1-loop integral with 6 free Lorenz indices:

\displaystyle I_{6}^{ijklmn}=\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{k^{i}k^{j}k^{k}k^{l}k^{m}k^{n}}{\mathbf{k}^{2}-k_{0}^{2}}

(3.18)

It can be written in terms of 15 form factors as:

\displaystyle I_{6}^{ijklmn}=\sum_{a}F_{a}g_{Fa}^{ijklmn}

(3.19)

where
g_{F}^{ijklmn}
is a 15 components vector defined as:

\displaystyle g_{F}^{ijklmn}=

\displaystyle(

\displaystyle\delta^{ij}\delta^{kl}\delta^{mn},\delta^{ij}\delta^{km}\delta^{ln},\delta^{ij}\delta^{kn}\delta^{ml},\delta^{ik}\delta^{jl}\delta^{mn},\delta^{ik}\delta^{jm}\delta^{ln},\delta^{ik}\delta^{jn}\delta^{ml},\delta^{il}\delta^{kj}\delta^{mn},\delta^{il}\delta^{mj}\delta^{kn},

(3.20)

\displaystyle\delta^{il}\delta^{nj}\delta^{mk},\delta^{im}\delta^{kl}\delta^{jn},\delta^{im}\delta^{kn}\delta^{jl},\delta^{im}\delta^{nl}\delta^{jm},\delta^{in}\delta^{kl}\delta^{mj},\delta^{in}\delta^{km}\delta^{lj},\delta^{in}\delta^{ml}\delta^{kj},)^{T}

As in the previous case we can obtain form factors by contracting
I_{6}^{ijklmn}
with appropriate projectors that have the following ansatz:

\displaystyle P^{ijklmn}_{a}=\sum_{b}C_{ab}g_{Fb\ ijklmn}\qquad with\ a=1\ldots 15

(3.21)

where the coefficients can be fixed by solving the following system of equations:

\displaystyle P_{a}^{ijklmn}g_{F\ ijklmn}=V_{a}

(3.22)

where and
V_{a}
is a unit vector with 15 components with values 1 in the
a
position and
0
in the rest.
After performing appropriately the tensor decomposition, we can express our integrals as a linear combination of form factors multiplying products of metric tensors.

3.2
Classification of Feynman integrals and reduction to scalar integrals

Now that we dealt with tensor structure, let us classify a generic Feynman integrals.

A typical
L
-loop Feynman integral, in
d
space-time dimensions, which appear in a form factor, is given by:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}=\int\prod_{i=1}^{L}\biggl[\frac{d^{d}k_{i}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\biggr]\frac{\mathcal{N}(k_{i},p_{j})}{D_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots D_{m}^{\alpha_{m}}}\ ,

(3.23)

where
k_{i}
are the loop momenta,
p_{i}
are external momenta and
m
is the number of denominators corresponding to internal lines of the diagrams.

Any diagram with
n
external legs, because of momentum conservation depends only on
n-1
momenta. The number
N
of possible scalar products between loop momenta,
k_{i}\cdot k_{j}
, and loop momenta and external momenta,
k_{i}\cdot p_{j}
, can be computed as:

\displaystyle N=L(n-1)+\frac{L(L+1)}{2}=L\left(n+\frac{L+1}{2}\right)\ ,

(3.24)

where
L(n-1)
is the number of scalar products between the
L
loop momenta and the
n-1
independent external momenta, whereas
L(L+1)/2
is the number of scalar products involving loop momenta only.
For
L>1
the number of scalar products can exceed the number of denominators of the diagram. Therefore, there are some scalar products which can be written in terms of denominators, the so-called
reducible scalar products
(RSPs), and other which cannot be written in terms of denominators, dubbed
irreducible scalar products
(ISPs).

We can easily deal with ISPs by artificially enlarge the set of denominators appearing, introducing
auxiliary denominators
, such that every scalar product can be written in terms of denominators.

Consequently, each scalar product in the numerator can be completely written in terms of the enlarged set of propagators, such that a generic Feynman integral can be written as a sum of scalar integrals:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{i}I_{i}\ ,

(3.25)

\displaystyle I_{i}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\prod_{i=1}^{L}\biggl[\frac{d^{d}k_{i}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\biggr]\mathcal{I}_{i}=\int\prod_{i=1}^{L}\biggl[\frac{d^{d}k_{i}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\biggr]\frac{1}{D_{1}^{\alpha_{i1}}\cdots D_{m}^{\alpha_{in}}}\ .

(3.26)

Before proceeding further let us fix some definitions that will be useful in the following:

•

Integral family: the set of denominators spanning the complete space of scalar products,

•

topology: a subset of the integral family, where all powers of the denominators are positive, and which identifies a graph with momentum conservation at each vertex,

•

sub-topology: a subset of the topology.

3.3
Decomposition of a Feynman diagram in Master Integrals

Now that we have written a generic form factor in terms of scalar integrals, we want to express all integrals appearing in terms of a smaller set of independent integrals, known as
master integrals
. The master integrals
\mathbf{I}^{MI}
are a basis of integrals in dimensional regularization.

An amplitude can be decomposed in terms of master Integrals as:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}=\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}I_{i}=\sum_{i}c_{i}\mathbf{I}_{i}^{MI}

(3.27)

The evaluation of a generic multi-loop amplitude then is achieved in two steps:

•

reduction
: decomposition in terms of MIs. This amount to determine the coefficients
c_{i}
of each MI
\mathbf{I}_{i}^{MI}
.

•

MIs
evaluation
: the actual calculation of the MI
\mathbf{I}_{i}^{MI}

3.3.1
Reduction to Master Integrals

Most of the Feynman integrals in a topology are related one to each other by relations that are due to
symmetry relations
,
Lorentz invariance identities
and
integration-by-parts
identities.

These relations are due to general properties of Feynman integrals, such as graph symmetries, Lorentz invariance of scalar functions, and to invariance under loop momenta redefinition of the integrals.
By using these relations we are able to express all integrals within any topology in terms of a basis of master integrals.

Symmetry Relations

The first set of relations between different integrals can be derived from trivial relabeling of the loop momenta (shifts), which leave the value of the integral unchanged since they have a trivial Jacobian.

Two classes of transformations are particularly useful:

•

the set of transformations that maps different topologies into each other, which allow us to decrease the number of independent topologies,

•

the set of transformations that map each topology onto itself, that allow us to derive identities between integrals within the same topology.

Lorentz Invariance Identities (LI)

Our scalar integrals
I_{i}
are Lorentz scalars, therefore they are invariant under all Lorentz transformations.

In particular, under an infinitesimal shift of the external momenta:

\displaystyle p_{i}^{\mu}\to p_{i}^{\mu}+w^{\mu\nu}p_{i,\nu},

(3.28)

where
w^{\mu\nu}
is a totally antisymmetric tensor, our Feynman integral transforms as:

\displaystyle I_{i}\to\biggl(1+w^{\mu\nu}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}p_{i,\mu}\frac{\partial}{\partial_{\mu}}\biggr)I_{i}

(3.29)

From Lorentz invariance of the latter expression one can obtain relations of the form:

\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\biggl(p_{i,\mu}\frac{\partial}{\partial_{i}^{\nu}}-p_{i,\nu}\frac{\partial}{\partial_{i}^{\mu}}\biggr)I_{i}=0,

(3.30)

which can be contracted with all possible symmetric tensors built from the external momenta, like
p_{j}^{\mu}p_{k}^{\nu}
.
The differentiation acting at the integrand level will generate integrals with different powers of denominators, which can be used as non-trivial relations among them called
Lorentz invariance identities
(LIs).

Integration by parts identities (IBP)

The most important set of identities that we will use are the integration-by-parts identities.

A generic Feynman integral is invariant under the redefinition of the loop momenta
k_{i}
, with
i=1,\ldots,L
, which may also involve any combination of loop and external momenta
p_{j}
, with
j=1,\cdots,n-1
:

k_{i}^{\mu}\to A_{ij}k_{j}^{\mu}+B_{ij}p_{j}^{\mu}.

(3.31)

By considering the action of infinitesimal transformations:

\displaystyle k_{i}^{\mu}\to k_{i}^{\mu}+\beta_{ij}q_{j}^{\mu}\ ,\qquad q_{j}=(k_{1},\cdots,k_{L},p_{1},\cdots p_{n-1}),

(3.32)

the integrand transforms as:

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{i}\to\biggl(1+\beta_{ij}q_{j}\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial_{q_{i}}}\biggr)\mathcal{I}_{i}.

(3.33)

If
j=i
, then also the integration measure changes as:

\displaystyle d^{d}k_{i}\to(1+\beta_{ii}d)d^{d}k_{i}\ ,

(3.34)

because
\partial k_{i}^{\mu}/\partial k_{j}^{\mu}=d\delta_{ij}
. We can combine these results in a single equation:

\displaystyle I_{i}=\int\prod_{i=1}^{L}d^{d}k_{i}\mathcal{I}_{\hskip 16.38895pt}\to\qquad\int\prod_{i=1}^{L}d^{d}k_{i}\biggl(1+\beta_{ij}\frac{\partial}{\partial k_{i}^{\mu}}q_{j}^{\mu}\biggr)\mathcal{I}_{i}\ .

(3.35)

The invariance of the integral implies:

\displaystyle\int\prod_{i=1}^{L}d^{d}k_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial k_{i}^{\mu}}\bigl(q_{j}^{\mu}\mathcal{I}_{i}\bigr)=0\ ,

(3.36)

where
q_{j}^{\mu}
is any linear combination of vectors chosen between the external legs or the integration momenta.

The differentiation acting on the integrand will generate integrals with different powers of denominators, which can be used as non-trivial relations among them, called integration-by-parts identities (IBPs).
These relations can be solved to write the initial scalar integrals in terms of more simple ones, that are the so-called
Master Integrals
.
The procedure has been implemented by Laporta
[
57
]
developing a method for high precision calculations of multi-loop, and it has been used in several works.

3.3.2
Master Integral evaluation

The third step of this procedure consists in the evaluation of the Master Integrals.

There are different ways to compute the Master Integrals: we can use direct integration (Feynman parameters, Schwinger parameters,
\ldots
), but when it becomes prohibitive one can use
differential equations
or
difference equations
.

Evaluation of massive tadpole via direct integration

We can compute the massive tadpole integral via direct integration.

d
-dimensions:

(3.37)

We can rewrite it, with the following change of variables:

\displaystyle k^{2}=\frac{p^{2}}{m^{2}}\ ,\qquad d^{d}k=(m^{2})^{\frac{d-2}{2}}m^{2}d^{d}k\ ,

(3.38)

obtaining

\displaystyle I_{1}(d)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(m^{2})^{\frac{d-2}{2}}\int d^{d}k\frac{1}{k^{2}+1}=(m^{2})^{\frac{d-2}{2}}X(d)\ .

(3.39)

Let us rewrite the integration measure appearing in
X(d)
in spherical coordinates, integrating over the
d-1
solid angle we obtain:

\displaystyle d^{d}k=\Omega_{d-1}k^{d-1}dk\ ,\qquad\Omega_{d-1}=\frac{2\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)}\ .

(3.40)

Then we perform the change of variables:

\displaystyle t=k^{2}\ ,\qquad dt=2kdk\ ,\qquad\to\qquad k^{d-1}dk=\frac{1}{2}t^{\frac{d-2}{2}}dt\ ,

(3.41)

obtaining:

\displaystyle X(d)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\Omega_{d-1}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}dt\frac{t^{\frac{d-2}{2}}}{t+1}

(3.42)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\Omega_{d-1}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{1}{2}\beta\left(\frac{d}{2},1-\frac{d}{2}\right)\ ,

where we introduced the Euler’s
\beta
function, defined as:

\displaystyle\beta(x,y)=\int_{0}^{\infty}dt\frac{t^{x-1}}{(1+t)^{x+y}}=\frac{\Gamma[x]\Gamma[y]}{\Gamma[x+y]}\ .

(3.43)

Then the integral becomes:

\displaystyle X(d)=\frac{2\pi^{\frac{d}{2}}}{\Gamma(d/2)}\frac{1}{2(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{\Gamma(d/2)\Gamma(1-d/2)}{\Gamma(1)}=\frac{1}{(4\pi)^{d/2}}\Gamma\left(1-\frac{d}{2}\right)\ .

(3.44)

Eventually we find:

\displaystyle I_{1}(d)=\hbox to29.25pt{\vbox to34.09pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip-5.29056pt\lower-17.04361pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

(3.45)

Vanishing of the massless tadpole

Using the calculation done for the massive case we can show in a simple way that the
massless tadpole
is vanishing:

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{d}k}{k^{2}}=0

(3.46)

This is somehow obvious in the framework of dimensional regularization, since it is a scaleless integral.

Let us compute the following integral:

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{d}k}{k^{2}(k+1)^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\Omega_{d-1}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt\frac{t^{\frac{d}{2}-2}}{t+1}=\frac{1}{2}\Gamma_{d-1}\beta\left(\frac{d}{2}-1,2-\frac{d}{2}\right)

(3.47)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\Omega_{d-1}\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}-1\right)\Gamma\left(2-\frac{d}{2}\right)=-\frac{1}{2}\Omega_{d-1}\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(1-\frac{d}{2}\right)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\int\frac{d^{d}k}{k^{2}+1}

but we have also:

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{d}k}{k^{2}(1+k^{2})}=\int\frac{d^{d}k}{k^{2}}-\int\frac{d^{d}k}{k^{2}+1}

(3.48)

hence we should have:

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{d}k}{k^{2}}=0

(3.49)

3.3.3
Direct evaluation of sunrise integral

We are interested in evaluating the following scalar integral in
d-
dimensions:

I_{S}(d,a,b)=\int\frac{d^{d}k}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{1}{k^{2a}(k^{2}+\Delta)^{b}}

(3.50)

Here
a,b
and
\Delta
are arbitrary real numbers, for which the integral could converge or not, while the
k
terms in the integrand stands for the Euclidean norm of
\mathbf{k}
.
In order to perform the evaluation we split the integration
\mathbb{R}^{d}
using spherical coordinates in
d
dimension:

\displaystyle I_{S}(d,a,b)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{d\Omega_{d}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\int_{0}^{\infty}dk\frac{k^{d-1}}{k^{2a}(k^{2}+\Delta)^{d}}

(3.51)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{2^{1-d}\pi^{-d/2}}{\Gamma[d/2]}\int_{0}^{+\infty}\ dk\frac{k^{d-1-2a}}{(k^{2}+\Delta)^{b}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{2^{1-d}\pi^{-d/2}}{\Gamma[d/2]}I_{|k|}(d,a,b)

(3.52)

\displaystyle I_{|k|}(d,a,b)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{+\infty}\ dk\frac{k^{d-1-2a}}{(k^{2}+\Delta)^{b}}\ .

(3.53)

As done for the tadpole case, we can collect the
\Delta
term in (
3.53
), and perform a rescaling in the variable of integration in order to obtain:

I_{|k|}(d,a,b)=\int_{0}^{+\infty}dk\frac{k^{d-1-2a}}{(k^{2}+\Delta)^{b}}=\Delta^{d/2-a-b}\int_{0}^{+\infty}dk\frac{k^{d-1-2a}}{(k^{2}+1)^{b}}

(3.54)

Introducing the change of coordinates
k=\sqrt{x}
, the following identities hold:

\int_{0}^{+\infty}dk\frac{k^{d-1-2a}}{(k^{2}+1)^{b}}=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{+\infty}dx\frac{x^{d/2-a-1}}{(x+1)^{b}}=\frac{1}{2}\beta\biggl(\frac{d}{2}-a,a+b-\frac{d}{2}\biggr)

(3.55)

where in the last equivalence we have introduced the
\beta-
function, as defined in Eq.(
3.43
). Inserting (
3.55
) into (
3.54
), we arrive at the final expression for (
3.53
):

I_{|k|}(d,a,b)=\Delta^{\frac{d}{2}-a-b}\frac{\Gamma[d/2-a]\Gamma[a+b-d/2]}{2\Gamma[b]}\ ,

(3.56)

and so (
3.51
) becomes:

I_{s}(d,a,b)=\frac{\Delta^{d/2-a-b}}{(4\pi)^{d/2}}\frac{\Gamma[d/2-a]\Gamma[a+b-d/2]}{\Gamma[b]\Gamma[d/2]}\ .

(3.57)

3.4
The scalar integral
I_{F}(d,a)

All our calculations will be made in Fourier space, and in order to give back a contribution to the effective action, we will have to perform a Fourier transform.

Is then necessary to evaluate a class of scalar integral regarded as a Fourier transform. The simplest, is the following Euclidean
d-
dimensional integral:

I_{F}(d,a)=\int\ \frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{e^{iq\cdot r}}{q^{2a}}\ .

(3.58)

Let us assume that
\vec{r}
represents a
d-
dimensional
z-
axis, we then decompose the measure of integration as:

d^{d}q=dq_{z}d^{d-1}Q_{\perp}=dq_{z}dQQ^{d-2}d\Omega_{d-1}\ ,

(3.59)

where
Q_{\perp}
is orthogonal to
q_{z}
, which is parallel to
\vec{r}
, while
Q
stand for its Euclidean norm.

Using (
3.59
), the previous integral becomes:

I_{F}(d,a)=\frac{\Omega_{d-1}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}dq_{z}\int_{0}^{+\infty}dQQ^{d-2}\frac{e^{iq_{z}r}}{(q_{z}^{2}+Q^{2})^{a}}\ .

(3.60)

At this point it is useful to introduce the following change of coordinates on the
(q_{z},Q)
upper-half plane:

\begin{cases}q_{z}=xQ\\
Q=\frac{y}{xr}\end{cases}\qquad\rightarrow\qquad\begin{cases}q_{z}=\frac{y}{r}\\
Q=\frac{y}{xr}\end{cases}\ ,

(3.61)

which is a map form
\mathcal{R}_{q_{z}}\times\mathcal{R}^{+}_{Q}
to
R^{2}_{x,y}
with determinant
\frac{y}{(xr)^{2}}
.
Applying this change to our integral gives:

I_{F}(d,a)=\frac{\Omega_{d-1}}{(2\pi)^{d}}r^{2a-d}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}dx\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}dy\frac{e^{iy}}{(y^{2})^{1/2-d/2+a}}\frac{x^{2a-d}}{(1+x^{2})^{a}}\ ,

(3.62)

which can be reduced to the product of two scalar integrals as:

I_{F}(d,a)=\frac{\Omega_{d-1}}{(2\pi)^{d}}r^{2a-d}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}dx\frac{x^{2a-d}}{(1+x^{2})^{a}}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}dy\frac{e^{iy}}{(y^{2})^{1/2-d/2+a}}\ .

(3.63)

The integral in the
x
variable can be easily performed by noticing that it is equivalent to a 1-loop sunrise integral (Eq.(
3.57
))with
d=\Delta=1
:

\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}dx\frac{x^{2a-d}}{(1+x^{2})^{a}}=\frac{\Gamma[a-d/2+1/2]\Gamma[(d-1)/2]}{2\Gamma[a]}\ .

(3.64)

We are left with the integral on the second bracket which comes from the more general one:

L(\alpha)=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}dy\frac{e^{iy}}{y^{\alpha}}\ ,

(3.65)

for a specific choice of
\alpha
.

The integral Eq.(
3.65
) can be evaluated using integration by parts, assuming
\alpha\in\mathbb{N}
, in order to derive a useful recurrence relation:

L(\alpha+1)=\frac{iL(\alpha)}{\alpha}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad L(\alpha)=\frac{i^{\alpha-1}}{\Gamma[\alpha]}L(1)\ ,

(3.66)

where
L(1)
is given by the principal value of a contour integral in the complex plane.

To show this, let us first define the line of integration by means of a counterclockwise closed curve avoiding
z=0
given by
\Omega=\{\Omega_{R}\cup(\mathbb{R}/[-r,+r])\cup\Omega_{r}\}
where
\Omega_{r}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}|z=re^{i\phi},0\leq\phi\leq\pi\}
, the same for
\Omega_{R}
.

Since the integrand of
L(1)
is a meromorphic function inside
\Omega
, one has:

\oint_{\Omega}\frac{e^{iz}}{z}=\int_{\Omega_{R}}\frac{e^{iz}}{z}dz+\int_{\mathbb{R}/[-r,r]}\frac{e^{iz}}{z}dz+\int_{\Omega_{r}}\frac{e^{iz}}{z}dz=0\ .

(3.67)

Now, sending
R\to\infty
the first integral is zero by means of Jordan’s lemma, while the second is equal to
L(1)
given that
r\to 0
. This means that:

L(1)=-\lim_{r\to 0}\int_{\Omega_{r}}\frac{e^{iz}}{z}dz

(3.68)

Integral (
3.68
) is easily evaluated using the fact that in the integration region
r
is fixed,
0\leq\phi\leq\pi
, and
dz=izd\phi
:

L(1)=-i\lim_{r\to 0}\int_{\pi}^{0}e^{ir(cos(\phi)+isin(\phi)}d\phi=-\int_{\pi}^{0}d\phi=i\pi\ .

(3.69)

The result is:

\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}dy\frac{e^{iy}}{y^{\alpha}}=\frac{\pi i^{\alpha}}{\Gamma[\alpha]}\ ,\qquad\alpha\in\mathbb{N}\ .

(3.70)

In order to relate (
3.70
) to
the integral in Eq.(
3.63
), we restrict ourselves to even
\alpha
since the integrand we are looking for depend on
y^{2}
, not
y
only.
With this choice, we can set
\alpha=2n
with
n=a+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{d}{2}
into (
3.70
), which gives via analytic continuation into
a
and
d
the following result:

\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}dy\frac{e^{iy}}{(y^{2})^{a+1/2-d/2}}=\frac{\pi(-1)^{a+1/2-d/2}}{\Gamma[2a+1-d]}\ .

(3.71)

Inserting (
3.71
),(
3.64
) into (
3.63
), after few manipulations with the Gamma function involved, one can prove that our scalar integral is equal to:

I_{F}(d,a)=\frac{\Gamma[d/2-a]}{(4\pi)^{d/2}\Gamma[a]}\left(\frac{r}{2}\right)^{2a-d}\ .

(3.72)

Chapter 4
Hereditary Effects in the EFT approach

Now that we have shown how to systematically compute multi-loop Feynman integrals, on this chapter we will evaluate far-zone contributions to the conservative dynamics, known as
Hereditary effects
, up to 5PN order. The hereditary effects, whose importance has been first noticed in
[
77
]
, are the influences of the past evolution of a material system on its present gravitational internal dynamics, and with such terms the dynamic of the binary system depend on the full past history of the source.

They are due to gravitational waves emitted by the system in the past and subsequently scattered-off the curvature of space-time back into the system. Such radiative terms give unavoidable contributions to the conservative binary dynamics, and it is mandatory to deal appropriately with this kind of processes in order to compute higher order PN corrections.
They can be classified in 3 different types of terms known as
Back-scattering
,
Tail-Effects
,
Memory Effects
:

(a)

(b)

(c)

(d)

Figure 4.1
:
The diagrams appear in the computation of Hereditary Effects. Diagram
(a)
is known as back-reaction, diagram
(b)
is a tail term whereas diagrams
(c)
and
(d)
are memory effects. In order to distinguish between
(c)
and
(d)
we will refer to diagram
(d)
as double emission. The double thick line denotes the multipole source, whereas curly and dashed lined correspond to gravitons coupled to time-dependent or conserved multipoles, respectively

•

Back-scattering
processes: diagram
(a)
in Fig.
4.1
, are processes where a gravitational wave is emitted by the binary system and then reabsorbed into the same GW source. They are the lowest-order contributions to the effective action, but as we will show they do not affect the conservative dynamics, but they only contribute to the dissipative one.

•

Tail terms
: diagram
(b)
in Fig.
4.1
, are processes where a Gravitational Wave is emitted by the binary system and scattered off the quasi-static curvature into the same GW source. The dotted line denotes a graviton attached to a conserved charge, which imply that the corresponding Green’s function has
exactly zero
time component momentum. They contribute to the conservative dynamics starting at 4PN as first noticed in
[
78
,
79
]
, and in the context of EFT in
[
52
]
.

•

Memory terms
: diagram
(c)
and
(d)
in Fig.
4.1
, are processes where a GW is emitted by the binary system and scattered off the curvature induced by GW themselves. In that case all the gravitons are attached to dynamical multipoles, and we must pay attention in addressing their computation. They contribute to the conservative dynamics starting at 5PN as first noticed in
[
137
]
in the context of linearized gravity, and then in
[
138
]
. In order to distinguish between the two diagrams, we will refer to diagram
(d)
as double emission.

State of the art

The computation of Hereditary Effects in the EFT approach was started in
[
80
]
, where it has been computed the LO radiation reaction effect at 2.5PN, and then at 3.5PN in
[
81
]
. Tail effects were computed at 4PN in
[
82
,
38
,
83
]
, at 5PN in
[
84
,
75
]
, and then extended to
d-
dimensional multipoles following
[
85
]
, and for all multipoles, in
[
86
]
. Tail of tail effects have been computed up to 7PN order in
[
88
]
. Memory effects instead have been computed at 5PN order in
[
84
,
75
,
87
]
. Conservative contributions coming from hereditary effects at 4PN order, and in particular the cancellation of IR divergences arising in intermediate stages have been studied in
[
83
,
89
,
90
,
68
,
91
]
.

The EFT approach is not the only way of computing hereditary effects. An analogous derivation has been performed from the "Tutti Frutti" approach
[
28
,
139
]
, and presented in
[
93
]
, and using PM techniques
[
94
,
140
,
141
]
.
However, at 5PN order, the different results proposed
[
87
,
75
,
93
,
94
]
do not agree in the prediction of physical observables like the two-body scattering angle. The 5PN dynamics is not fully understood at the moment, and there are several subtle puzzles that needs to be studied and understood before proceeding in the evaluation of higher order PN corrections.

Goals of the chapter

The goal of this chapter is to perform an independent derivation of the hereditary processes up to 5PN order, to verify the results proposed in
[
84
]
, and later explained in
[
87
]
and
[
86
]
, and the ones computed in
[
75
]
. We want to shed new light in the computation of these processes, by constructing a new computational algorithm in Mathematica which starting from the effective action in the far zone introduced in Eq.(
2.147
), computes the Feynman rules, generate the diagrams and evaluates them using modern multi-loop techniques, and which can be generalized at arbitrary PN order.
From the multipole action (
2.147
) we can generate a wide variety of triple multipole diagrams following the power counting rules described in the previous chapter
2.7.6
.

The lowest contributing terms are those containing two electric quadrupole moments, because
E
and
L_{k}
are conserved in the stationary case we are considering.
We will consider the following diagrams:

•

QQ
, which is of order
\mathcal{O}(v^{7})
, and contributes at lowest order at 2.5 PN,

•

QEQ
, which is of order
\mathcal{O}(v^{10})
and contributes at lowest order at 4PN,

•

QLQ
,
JEJ
,
OEO
and
QQQ
which are of order
\mathcal{O}(v^{12})
and contributes at lowest order at 5PN.

4.1
The method

The complete evaluation of the Hereditary terms reported in Fig.
4.1
has been performed using Mathematica, following a systematic procedure that we will now present.
The generic contribution to the effective action is of the form:

S_{eff}=-i\lim_{d\to 3}A_{her}\ ,

where

:

\mathcal{M}_{i}=\sum_{j}c_{ij}I_{j}^{M.I.}

\mathcal{M}=\sum_{i}\mathcal{M}_{i}=\sum_{j}c_{j}I^{M.I.}_{j}

Figure 4.2
:
Flow chart of the algorithm for the evaluation of Hereditary Effects

4.1.1
Integrand generation

The diagrams appearing in figure
4.1
are only
skeleton diagrams
, and propagating lines denote generic gravitational fields without specifying the polarization
\phi,A,\sigma
. In particular, green curly lines denote couplings to time-dependent multipoles whereas blue dashed lines denote gravitons coupled to conserved quantities such as the energy and the angular momentum. If we want to compute them we need to
specify the polarization
of the fields, and by doing so we obtain a linear combination of several diagrams with appropriate symmetry factors.
We need then to substitute the explicit expressions of the
Feynman Rules
, which are reported in Appendix.
A
, for propagators, triple graviton vertices, and multipoles couplings. We can then perform tensor contractions using the package xAct
[
142
]
. Following the key observation made in the previous chapter in eq.(
2.153
), since the source is static and do not propagate, any amplitude can be mapped into a
multi-loop 1 point function
with massive internal lines, where the masses are the energy components of the propagators:
D(k)=\frac{1}{\mathbf{k}^{2}-k_{0}^{2}}
. Once this identification has been made, we can evaluate amplitudes using multi-loop techniques.

\mathcal{M}_{her}^{Q_{n}}
turns out to have the following structure:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{her}^{Q_{n}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\biggl[\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k_{i}}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\biggr]Q^{(1)}_{J_{1}}(k_{10})\cdots Q^{(n)}_{J_{n}}(k_{n0})\frac{N^{J_{1}\cdots J_{n}}(\mathbf{k}_{1},\cdots\mathbf{k}_{n},k_{10},\cdots k_{n0})}{D_{1}D_{2}\ldots D_{n}}

(4.4)

where:

•

J_{i}=j_{i1},...j_{il_{i}}

•

Q^{(i)}_{J_{1}}(k_{i0})
denotes the Fourier-transform of a generic multipole moment,

•

\mathbf{k_{i}}
are the loop momenta,
k_{i0}
are the energy components.

•

N^{J_{1},\cdots J_{N}}
is a generic tensorial numerator,

•

D_{i}=(\mathbf{k_{i}}^{2}-k_{i0}^{2})
, where
k_{n}=-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}k_{i}
, are the denominators coming from the propagators.

Since we are dealing with radiative gravitons and not with potential ones, the scalings of momentum components are:
\left(k_{0},|\mathbf{k}|\right)\approx\left(\frac{v}{r},\frac{v}{r}\right)
. We cannot take anymore the non-relativistic expansion of the propagators, and so we treat the energy components of loop momenta as effective masses, and we integrate over the spatial components of the momenta.

4.1.2
Tensor decomposition

Since we are dealing with tensorial quantities we need to appropriately decompose tensor integrals in terms of form factors as explained in Sec.
3.1
. Moreover, since multipoles are symmetric trace free tensors and there are no external momenta, the tensor decomposition will be hugely simplified and in the end all multipoles will be contracted among each others, obtaining an expression of the form:

\mathcal{M}_{her}^{Q^{n}}=Tr[Q_{1}\cdots Q_{n}]\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_{her}^{Q^{n}}

(4.5)

4.1.3
Integrand reduction

Once we obtain a form factor of the form
\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_{her}^{Q^{n}}
, we need to rewrite it in terms of scalar integrals. In order to do that, we need to rewrite the scalar products appearing in the numerator of our integrand in terms of denominators, and then expand the expression to get a sum of scalar integrals:

\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_{her}^{Q^{n}}=\sum_{i}b_{i}I_{i}

(4.6)

4.1.4
IBP Decomposition

In order to get the result we need to decompose the form factor written in scalar integrals
\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_{her}^{Q^{n}}
in terms of Master Integrals, using the package Litered
[
143
]
, as:

\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_{her}^{Q^{n}}\ =\ \sum_{i}C_{i}J_{i}^{MI}

(4.7)

4.1.5
Results

We can then substitute the explicit expression for the MIs, and expand around
d=3
to obtain a correction to the effective action:

\displaystyle S_{eff}=-i\lim_{d\to 3}A_{her}

(4.8)

4.2
Back-scattering at leading order

In this section we will evaluate the 1-loop back-scattering process at leading order.

As we will see this diagram will not contribute to the conservative dynamics, but only to the dissipative one. This diagram contains a single radiation graviton. Hence, as discussed in Sec.
2.4.3
and in
[
87
]
, using Feynman propagator we will get the correct answer for the contribution to the conservative dynamics, and we will proceed by doing so. It contains two electric quadrupole moments
Q
:

Q_{ij}
Q_{kl}

\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad

:

Contributing diagrams

In order to compute the effective diagrams we need to specify the polarisations of the graviton fields and sum up all the non-vanishing combinations.

There are 3 diagrams contributing, where we substitute, respectively, the fields
\phi,A,\sigma

\lxSVG@closescope {{{}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}

(4.12)

The total amplitude is given by:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{Q^{2}}=\mathcal{M}_{\phi}^{Q^{2}}+\mathcal{M}_{A}^{Q^{2}}+\mathcal{M}_{\sigma}^{Q^{2}}

(4.13)

where:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\phi}^{Q^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\left(T_{Q\phi}(-\mathbf{k},-k_{0})T_{Q\phi}(\mathbf{k},k_{0})P_{\phi}(\mathbf{k},k_{0})\right)\ ,

(4.14)

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{A}^{Q^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\left(T_{QA}^{i}(-\mathbf{k},-k_{0})T_{QA}^{j}(\mathbf{k},k_{0})P_{Aij}(\mathbf{k},k_{0})\right)\ ,

(4.15)

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\sigma}^{Q^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\left(T_{Q\sigma}^{ij}(-\mathbf{k},-k_{0})T_{Q\sigma}^{kl}(\mathbf{k},k_{0})^{kl}P_{\phi ijkl}(\mathbf{k},k_{0})\right)\ .

(4.16)

Substituting the appropriate Feynman rules and applying tensor contractions using xTensor we get:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\phi}^{Q^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{i(d-2)}{16(d-1)\Lambda^{2}}\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{k_{a}k_{b}k_{c}k_{d}}{D_{1}}Q^{ab}(k_{0})Q^{cd}(-k_{0})\ ,

(4.17)

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{A}^{Q^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{i}{8\Lambda^{2}}k_{0}^{2}\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{k_{a}k_{b}}{D_{1}}Q^{ac}(k_{0})Q_{c}^{b}(-k_{0})\ ,

(4.18)

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\sigma}^{Q^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{i}{16\Lambda^{2}}\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{1}{D_{1}}k_{0}^{4}Q_{ab}(k_{0})Q^{ab}(-k_{0})\ .

(4.19)

After applying tensor decomposition we obtain an expression of the form:

\mathcal{M}^{Q^{2}}=Q_{ab}(k_{0})Q^{ab}(-k_{0})\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{Q^{2}}

(4.20)

where
\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{Q^{2}}
is of the type:

\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{Q^{2}}\ =\ \frac{i}{32(d-1)d(d+2)\Lambda^{2}}\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{\left(d^{2}+d-2\right)k_{0}^{2}\left(d\ k_{0}^{2}-2\mathbf{k}^{2}\right)+2(d-2)\mathbf{k}^{4}}{D_{1}}

(4.21)

Integrand reduction

In order to get an expression in terms of scalar integrals, we need to rewrite the scalar products appearing in terms of denominators, which in this case can just be performed by substituting:

\mathbf{k}^{2}\ =\ D_{1}+k_{0}^{2}\ ,

(4.22)

and expanding the expression in order to obtain a linear combination of integrals.

IBP decomposition

We can now perform an IBP decomposition of the integrals appearing using Litered, to get an expression in terms of a single 1-loop Master Integral:

(4.23)

Coefficient

The coefficient is given by:

C_{1}^{Q^{2}}=\frac{(d-2)(d+1)}{32(d-1)(d+2)\Lambda^{2}}

(4.24)

j_{1}(k_{0})

(4.25)

Result

In order to get the contribution to the conservative dynamics we need to substitute the explicit expression for the MI, to write
d=3+\epsilon
, and to take the limit
\epsilon\to 0
as:

\displaystyle S^{Q^{2}}_{eff\ 2.5PN}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-i\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk_{0}}{(2\pi)}Q_{ij}(k_{0})Q^{ij}(-k_{0})\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{Q^{2}}

(4.26)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle i\frac{G_{N}}{10}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk_{0}}{(2\pi)}|k_{0}|k_{0}^{4}Q_{ij}(k_{0})Q^{ij}(-k_{0})

From (
4.26
), one can obtain the corresponding contribution in position space:

\displaystyle S_{eff\ 2.5PN}^{Q^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{G_{N}}{10}\int\ dt\ Q_{ij}(t)\frac{d^{5}}{dt^{5}}Q^{ij}(t)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{G_{N}}{20}\int\ dt\ \frac{d}{dt}\biggl(\ddot{Q}^{ij}(t)\ddot{Q}_{ij}(t)\biggr)

This is a total time derivative, which gives zero assuming that the multipoles moments and their derivatives vanish at infinity, and hence it does not contribute to the equations of motion for the conservative dynamics.

4.3
Tail Effects

This section will be dedicated to the evaluation of the tail diagrams.

Tail effects are due to gravitational waves emitted by the binary system and scattered off the quasi-static curvature onto the same gravitational-wave source.
The leading contribution to the conservative dynamics is at 4PN order, whereas the NLO is at 5PN. They are characterized by 3 multipoles, hence they can be seen as 2-loops one-point functions.

(4.28)

The main feature about tail effects is that one of the graviton is coupled to a conserved source, which is either the energy
E
of the system or the angular momentum
L_{i}
.
That means that we can send:

\displaystyle Q^{(1)}_{i_{1}\cdots i_{n}}(q_{0})\to(2\pi)\delta(q_{0})\tilde{Q}_{i_{1}\cdots i_{n}}^{(1)}

(4.29)

and the propagator of the corresponding line becomes instantaneous.
In this case the generic amplitude given in eq.(
4.4
) simplifies in:

\displaystyle A_{her}^{tail}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{dk_{0}}{(2\pi)}\frac{dq_{0}}{(2\pi)}\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{d}}Q^{(1)}_{i_{1}...i_{l}}(q_{0})Q^{(2)}_{j1,...,j_{m}}(k_{0})Q^{(3)}_{k_{1}...k_{n}}(p_{0})

\displaystyle\frac{N^{i_{1}...i_{l}\ j_{1}...j_{m}\ k_{1}...k_{n}}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q},k_{0},q_{0},p_{0})}{D_{1}D_{2}D_{3}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{dk_{0}}{(2\pi)}\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\tilde{Q}_{i_{1}...i_{l}}Q^{(2)}_{j1,...,j_{m}}(k_{0})Q^{(3)}_{k_{1}...k_{n}}(-k_{0})\frac{N^{i_{1}...i_{l}\ j_{1}...j_{m}\ k_{1}...k_{n}}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q},k_{0})}{(D_{1}D_{2}D_{3})\big|_{q_{0}=0}}

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{her}^{tail}

\displaystyle=

(4.31)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\tilde{Q}_{i_{1}...i_{l}}Q^{(2)}_{j1,...,j_{m}}(k_{0})Q^{(3)}_{k_{1}...k_{n}}(-k_{0})\frac{N^{i_{1}...i_{l}\ j_{1}...j_{m}\ k_{1}...k_{n}}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q},k_{0})}{(D_{1}D_{2}D_{3})\big|_{q_{0}=0}}\ ,

where the denominators appearing are defined as:

\displaystyle D_{1}=[\mathbf{k}^{2}-(k_{0})^{2}]\ ,\qquad D_{2}=[(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q})^{2}-(p_{0})^{2}]\ ,\qquad D_{3}=[\mathbf{q}^{2}-(q_{0})^{2}]\ ,

(4.32)

and once we take the limit
q_{0}\to 0
they collapse in:

\displaystyle D_{T1}=(\mathbf{k}^{2}-k_{0}^{2})\ ,\qquad D_{T2}=[(\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{q})^{2}-k_{0}^{2}]\ ,\qquad D_{T3}=\mathbf{q^{2}}\ .

(4.33)

In the computation of these diagrams we encounter two radiation propagators. Hence, as discussed in Sec.
2.4.3
, using Feynman propagators we will obtain the correct answer for the contribution to the conservative dynamics.

Contributing diagrams

In order to compute the effective diagrams we need to specify the polarisations of the graviton fields and sum up all the non-vanishing combinations.

In the case of a coupling to the effective mass
E
only the field
\phi
couples to
E
.

The symmetry factors can be fixed in the following way: we assign symmetry factor
1/2
to diagrams having identical polarizations coupled to
Q^{\prime}s
.

The total amplitude is given by:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{EQ^{2}}=\left(\mathcal{M}_{\phi\sigma^{2}}^{EQ^{2}}+\mathcal{M}_{\phi A\sigma}^{EQ^{2}}+\mathcal{M}_{\phi^{2}\sigma}^{EQ^{2}}+\mathcal{M}_{\phi A^{2}}^{EQ^{2}}+\mathcal{M}_{\phi^{2}A}^{EQ^{2}}+\mathcal{M}_{\phi^{3}}^{EQ^{2}}\right)

(4.35)

and the single components are given by:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\phi\sigma^{2}}^{EQ^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{d}}T_{Q\sigma}^{ij}(-\mathbf{k},-k_{0})T_{Q\sigma}^{kl}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},p_{0})T_{E\phi}(-\mathbf{q},-q_{0})

(4.36)

\displaystyle P_{\sigma ijmn}(\mathbf{k},k_{0})P_{\sigma klop}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},p_{0})P_{\phi}V_{\phi\sigma^{2}}^{mnop}(\mathbf{k},k_{0},\mathbf{q},q_{0})\ ,

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\phi A\sigma}^{EQ^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{d}}T_{QA}^{i}(-\mathbf{k},-k_{0})T_{Q\sigma}^{kl}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},p_{0})T_{E\phi}(-\mathbf{q},-q_{0})

(4.37)

\displaystyle P_{Aij}(\mathbf{k},k_{0})P_{\sigma klop}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},p_{0})P_{\phi}V_{\phi A\sigma}^{jop}(\mathbf{k},k_{0},\mathbf{q},q_{0})\ ,

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\phi^{2}\sigma}^{EQ^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{d}}T_{Q\sigma}^{ij}(-\mathbf{k},-k_{0})T_{Q\phi}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},p_{0})T_{E\phi}(-\mathbf{q},-q_{0})

(4.38)

\displaystyle P_{\sigma ijmn}(\mathbf{k},k_{0})P_{\phi}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},p_{0})P_{\phi}V_{\phi^{2}\sigma}^{mn}(\mathbf{k},k_{0},\mathbf{q},q_{0})\ ,

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\phi A^{2}}^{EQ^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{d}}T_{QA}^{i}(-\mathbf{k},-k_{0})T_{QA}^{k}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},p_{0})T_{E\phi}(-\mathbf{q},-q_{0})

(4.39)

\displaystyle P_{Aim}(\mathbf{k},k_{0})P_{Ako}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},p_{0})P_{\phi}V_{\phi\sigma^{2}}^{mo}(\mathbf{k},k_{0},\mathbf{q},q_{0})\ ,

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\phi^{2}A}^{EQ^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{d}}T_{QA}^{i}(-\mathbf{k},-k_{0})T_{Q\phi}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},p_{0})T_{E\phi}(-\mathbf{q},-q_{0})

(4.40)

\displaystyle P_{Aim}(\mathbf{k},k_{0})P_{\phi}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},p_{0})P_{\phi}V_{\phi^{2}A}^{m}(\mathbf{k},k_{0},\mathbf{q})\ ,

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\phi^{3}}^{EQ^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{d}}T_{Q\phi}(-\mathbf{k},-k_{0})T_{Q\phi}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},p_{0})T_{E\phi}(-\mathbf{q},-q_{0})

(4.41)

\displaystyle P_{\phi}(\mathbf{k},k_{0})P_{\phi}(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q},p_{0})P_{\phi}(\mathbf{q},q_{0})V_{\phi^{3}}(\mathbf{k},k_{0},\mathbf{q},q_{0})\ .

After applying tensor contractions and the tensor decomposition procedure we obtain an expression of the form:

\mathcal{M}^{EQ^{2}}=EQ_{ij}(k_{0})Q^{ij}(-k_{0})\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{EQ^{2}}

(4.42)

IBP Decomposition

Applying IBP decomposition on
\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{EQ^{2}}
we get an expression in terms of a single Master Integral:

\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{EQ^{2}}=C^{EQ^{2}}j_{T,1,1,0}

(4.43)

Coefficient

The coefficient is given by:

\displaystyle C^{EQ^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{k_{0}^{4}}{128\Lambda^{4}\epsilon(\epsilon+2)^{2}(\epsilon+3)(\epsilon+5)}\left(\epsilon^{5}+9\epsilon^{4}+31\epsilon^{3}+51\epsilon^{2}+52\epsilon+24\right)\ .

Result

After applying the reduction procedure outlined in the previous section we get:

\displaystyle S^{EQ^{2}}_{eff\ 4PN}=-\frac{G_{N}^{2}E}{5}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk_{0}}{(2\pi)}k_{0}^{6}\left[\frac{1}{\epsilon}-\frac{41}{30}-i\pi+\log\left(\frac{k_{0}^{2}}{\bar{\mu}^{2}}\right)+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)\right]Q_{ij}(k_{0})Q^{ij}(-k_{0})

(4.49)

where
\bar{\mu}^{2}=\mu^{2}\pi/e^{\gamma_{E}}
.
This result agrees with Eq.10 of
[
84
]

Divergent part

The divergent part of the tail amplitude receives contributions only from processes involving the same graviton polarizations attaching to the two radiative sources, as they are the ones diverging when
\mathbf{q}\to 0
.

The double integration over space momenta
\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}
on purely heuristic arguments, leads to an amplitude result
\sim G_{d}^{3}(-k_{0}^{2})^{d-3}
, from which we can infer that the presence of an imaginary part is invariably linked to a divergence:

\displaystyle\frac{G_{d}^{2}}{\epsilon}(-k_{0}^{2})^{\epsilon}=G_{N}^{2}\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}+\log\left(\frac{k_{0}^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)-i\pi+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)\right)

(4.50)

implying that pole residual not only fixes the logarithmic term but also the imaginary one.
The divergent part can be regularized by adding a similarly divergent term coming from the near zone dynamics as shown in
[
91
]
, with a procedure known as
zero-bin subtraction scheme
(see
[
49
]
for a generic treatment of cancellation of divergences using the method of regions)

4.3.2
Octupole Tail:
EO^{2}

The octupole Tail is contributing at 5PN to the conservative dynamics and it contains the multipoles
EO^{2}
:

E
O_{ijk}
O_{lmn}

Figure 4.5
:
Octupole tail

As in the previous case the multipole
E
is conserved.

The total amplitude is given by:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{EO^{2}}\ =\ \mathcal{M}^{EO^{2}}_{\phi\sigma^{2}}+\mathcal{M}^{EO^{2}}_{\phi A\sigma}+\mathcal{M}^{EO^{2}}_{\phi^{2}\sigma}+\mathcal{M}^{EO^{2}}_{\phi A^{2}}+\mathcal{M}^{EO^{2}}_{\phi^{2}A}+\mathcal{M}^{EO^{2}}_{\phi^{3}}

(4.52)

Result

After applying the reduction procedure outlined in the previous section we get:

\displaystyle S^{EO^{2}}_{eff\ 5PN}=-\frac{G_{N}^{2}E}{189}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk_{0}}{(2\pi)}k_{0}^{8}\left[\frac{1}{\epsilon}-\frac{82}{35}-i\pi+\log\left(\frac{k_{0}^{2}}{\bar{\mu}^{2}}\right)+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)\right]O_{ijk}(k_{0})O^{ijk}(-k_{0})

(4.53)

(4.54)

The total amplitude is given by:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{EJ^{2}}=\mathcal{M}^{EJ^{2}}_{\phi\sigma^{2}}+\mathcal{M}^{Ej^{2}}_{\phi A\sigma}+\mathcal{M}^{EJ^{2}}_{\phi A^{2}}

(4.55)

Result

After applying the reduction procedure outlined in the previous section we get:

\displaystyle S^{EJ^{2}}_{eff\ 5PN}=-\frac{16}{45}G_{N}^{2}E\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk_{0}}{(2\pi)}k_{0}^{6}\left[\frac{1}{\epsilon}-\frac{127}{60}-i\pi+\log\left(\frac{k_{0}^{2}}{\bar{\mu}^{2}}\right)+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)\right]J_{ij}(k_{0})J^{ij}(-k_{0})

(4.56)

This result agrees with Eq.21 of
[
84
]
.
A comment should be made before proceeding further. In the Feynman rules for the coupling of
\phi,A,\sigma
with the magnetic quadrupole tail
J_{ij}
,appears a Levi-Civita tensor
\epsilon_{ijk}
. Following the prescriptions given in
[
87
]
we assume that this
\epsilon_{ijk}
is 3-dimensional and no d-dimensional, hence we should be careful when contracting two Levi-Civita tensors in using the appropriate 3-dimensional rules. A
d
-dimensional generalization of this multipole has been proposed in
[
85
,
86
]
.

d-dimensional generalization

Following
[
85
,
86
]
, one can rewrite the magnetic quadrupole coupling appearing in Eq.(
2.147
) in d-dimensions, by specifying the magnetic component of the Riemann tensor defined in Eq.(
2.138
), and by making the following substitution:

S_{mult}\supset-\frac{2}{3}\int dtJ^{ij}B_{ij}=-\frac{1}{3}\int dtJ^{ij}\epsilon_{ikl}R_{0jkl}\ \ \to\ \ -\frac{1}{3}\int\ dtJ^{k|jl}R_{0jkl}\ ,

(4.57)

where
J^{k|jl}
is the d-dimensional generalization of the magnetic quadrupole, it is symmetric trace free and antisymmetric under
k\leftrightarrow l
, and in the limit
d\to 3
it reproduces the known coupling:

J^{k|jl}\ \overset{\mathrm{d=3}}{=}\ J^{ij}\epsilon_{ikl}\ .

(4.58)

By using this new coupling, one can recompute the magnetic quadrupole tail obtaining:

\displaystyle S^{EJ^{2}}_{eff\ 5PN}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{16}{135}G_{N}^{2}E\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk_{0}}{(2\pi)}k_{0}^{6}\left[\frac{1}{\epsilon}-\frac{49}{20}-i\pi+\log\left(\frac{k_{0}^{2}}{\bar{\mu}^{2}}\right)+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)\right]\times

(4.59)

\displaystyle\times\biggl(J_{i|jk}(k_{0})J^{i|jk}(-k_{0})+J_{i|jk}(k_{0})J^{j|ik}(-k_{0})\biggr)\ ,

which agrees with Eq.(9) of
[
86
]
.

4.3.4
Angular momentum "failed" tail:
LQ^{2}

The Angular momentum "failed" tail is contributing at 5PN to the conservative dynamics, and it contains the multipoles
LQ^{2}
:

L_{m}
Q_{ij}
Q_{kl}

Figure 4.7
:
Angular Momentum "failed" tail

In this case
L_{i}
is conserved and we can send:

\displaystyle L_{i}(q_{0})\to L_{i}(2\pi)\delta(q_{0})

(4.60)

and the propagator of the corresponding line becomes instantaneous.

Contributing diagrams

We need now to specify the polarizations, there are 6 diagrams contributing as only the
A
field couples with the angular momentum
L_{i}
:

L_{m}
Q_{ij}
Q_{kl}

The total amplitude is given by:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{LQ^{2}}\ =\ \mathcal{M}_{A\sigma^{2}}^{LQ^{2}}+\mathcal{M}_{\phi A\sigma}^{LQ^{2}}+\mathcal{M}_{A^{2}\sigma}^{LQ^{2}}+\mathcal{M}_{A^{3}}^{LQ^{2}}+\mathcal{M}_{\phi^{2}A}^{LQ^{2}}+\mathcal{M}_{A^{2}\phi}^{LQ^{2}}

(4.62)

Result

After applying the reduction procedure outlined in the previous section we get:

\displaystyle S^{LQ^{2}}_{eff\ 5PN}=-\frac{iG_{N}^{2}}{15}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk_{0}}{(2\pi)}k_{0}^{7}L_{m}\epsilon_{mik}Q_{ij}(k_{0})Q_{kj}(-k_{0})

(4.63)

and if we move in time domain the effective action becomes:

\displaystyle S^{LQ^{2}}_{eff\ 5PN}=-\frac{8}{15}G_{N}^{2}\int dt\ddddot{Q}_{ij}\dddot{Q}_{jl}\epsilon_{ijk}L_{k}

(4.64)

This result agrees with Eq.(24) of
[
84
]
, where we notice that we are using a different definition for the angular momentum
\vec{L}
, in particular:
\vec{L}=-\vec{L}^{Ref.[81]}
. This diagram involving the conserved angular momentum
\vec{L}
can be dubbed as "failed" tail because it gives just an instantaneous contribution to the conservative dynamics.

Indeed, for this diagram at least one of the graviton polarizations must be an
A
, and it presents a gradient coupling proportional to momentum
\mathbf{q}
that kills any divergence of the amplitude, which in the case of
q_{0}=0
occurs for
\mathbf{q}\to 0
.

Then all the diagrams involving the conserved quantity
\vec{L}
and any higher multipole are qualitatively different from the ones involving
E
in that the former are real, finite and local.

4.4
Memory Effects

Let us now compute the memory term diagram contributing at 5PN, which is the
QQQ
diagram.

In this case there are 3 mass quadrupoles, which are not conserved quantities, hence no simplification occurs.

Q_{mn}
Q_{ij}
Q_{kl}

Figure 4.8
:
Memory term

In this case the right description for the problem is the use of the in-in formalism since we are dealing with radiation. However, as discussed in Sec.
2.4.3
, we can deal with this problem by using retarded BC for two propagators and advanced for the third one.
Following
[
84
]
, we use retarded boundary conditions for
k,q
and advanced ones for
p
, and at the of the computation we will take
p_{0}=-k_{0}-q_{0}
.
The generic form of the amplitude in this case is:

\displaystyle A_{her}^{Q^{3}}

(4.65)

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{her}^{Q^{3}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{d}}Q^{(1)}_{i_{1}...i_{l}}(q_{0})Q^{(2)}_{j1,...,j_{m}}(k_{0})Q^{(3)}_{k_{1}...k_{n}}(p_{0})\frac{N^{i_{1}...i_{l}\ j_{1}...j_{m}\ k_{1}...k_{n}}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q},k_{0},q_{0},p_{0})}{D_{1}D_{2}D_{3}}

where the denominators are defined as:

\displaystyle D_{1}=[\mathbf{k}^{2}-(k_{0}+ia)^{2}]\ ,\qquad D_{2}=[(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q})^{2}-(p_{0}-ia)^{2}]\ ,\qquad D_{3}=[\mathbf{q}^{2}-(q_{0}+ia)^{2}]\ .

(4.66)

4.4.1
Contributing diagrams

There are 27 different diagrams contributing, but we can compute only 10 of them and symmetrize over the possible choices of momenta.

We will assign symmetry factor
1/2
for diagrams with 2 identical internal legs and
1/6
for diagrams with 3 identical graviton polarizations.

The corresponding contribution to the effective action is given by:

\displaystyle S_{EFF\ 5PN}^{Q^{3}}=-i\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk^{0}}{(2\pi)}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dq^{0}}{(2\pi)}\left(\mathcal{M}^{Q^{3}}\right)

(4.68)

where:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{Q^{3}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\biggl(V(k,p,q)+V(p,q,k)+V(q,k,p)\biggr)

(4.69)

\displaystyle V(k,p,q)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\biggl(\mathcal{M}_{\sigma^{3}}^{Q^{3}}+\mathcal{M}_{\sigma^{2}A}^{Q^{3}}+\mathcal{M}_{\sigma^{2}\phi}^{Q^{3}}+\mathcal{M}_{\phi A\sigma}^{Q^{3}}+\mathcal{M}_{\sigma A^{2}}^{Q^{3}}

(4.70)

\displaystyle+\mathcal{M}_{\sigma\phi^{2}}^{Q^{3}}+\mathcal{M}_{A^{3}}^{Q^{3}}+\mathcal{M}_{A^{2}\phi}^{Q^{3}}+\mathcal{M}_{A\phi^{2}}^{Q^{3}}+\mathcal{M}_{\phi^{3}}^{Q^{3}}\biggr)

We can substitute the Feynman rules, apply tensor contractions and tensor decomposition to get:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{Q^{3}}=Q_{ij}(k_{0})Q_{jk}(q_{0})Q_{ki}(p_{0})\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{Q^{3}}\ .

(4.71)

IBP decomposition

\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{Q^{3}}
is an expression in terms of scalar integrals, belonging to the same topology
j_{n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}}
defined as:

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}\ =\ \int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\int\frac{d^{d}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{1}{(D_{1})^{n_{1}}(D_{2})^{n_{2}}(D_{3})^{n_{3}}}\ ,

(4.72)

where, given the prescriptions for the propagators, the denominators are defined as:

\displaystyle D_{1}=[\mathbf{k}^{2}-(k_{0}+ia)^{2}]\ ,\qquad D_{2}=[(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q})^{2}-(p_{0}-ia)^{2}]\ ,\qquad D_{3}=[\mathbf{q}^{2}-(q_{0}+ia)^{2}]\ .

(4.73)

At this point we can IBP decompose the scalar integrals appearing, since this procedure is not affected by the choice of boundary conditions.

Coefficients

The coefficients, writing
d=3+\epsilon
are given by:

\displaystyle C_{1}^{Q^{3}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{k_{0}}{384\Lambda^{4}(\epsilon+2)^{2}(\epsilon+3)(\epsilon+5)(\epsilon+7)}\biggl[k_{0}^{3}q_{0}^{2}\left(\epsilon^{5}+18\epsilon^{4}+107\epsilon^{3}+308\epsilon^{2}+406\epsilon+200\right)

(4.75)

\displaystyle+2k_{0}^{2}q_{0}^{3}\left(\epsilon^{5}+18\epsilon^{4}+115\epsilon^{3}+351\epsilon^{2}+507\epsilon+284\right)

\displaystyle-2k_{0}^{4}q_{0}\left(8\epsilon^{3}+61\epsilon^{2}+163\epsilon+140\right)-2q_{0}^{5}\left(\epsilon^{3}+8\epsilon^{2}+19\epsilon+12\right)

\displaystyle-2k_{0}^{5}\left(4\epsilon^{3}+35\epsilon^{2}+97\epsilon+84\right)+k_{0}q_{0}^{4}\left(\epsilon^{5}+18\epsilon^{4}+113\epsilon^{3}+326\epsilon^{2}+438\epsilon+232\right)\biggr]

\displaystyle C_{2}^{Q^{3}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{k_{0}q_{0}}{384\Lambda^{4}(\epsilon+2)^{2}(\epsilon+3)(\epsilon+5)(\epsilon+7)}\biggl[2k_{0}^{2}q_{0}^{2}\bigl(\epsilon^{5}+18\epsilon^{4}+121\epsilon^{3}+381\epsilon^{2}+559\epsilon

(4.76)

\displaystyle+300\bigr)+k_{0}^{3}q_{0}\left(\epsilon^{5}+18\epsilon^{4}+123\epsilon^{3}+406\epsilon^{2}+628\epsilon+352\right)

\displaystyle+2k_{0}^{4}\left(\epsilon^{3}+8\epsilon^{2}+19\epsilon+12\right)+k_{0}q_{0}^{3}\left(\epsilon^{5}+18\epsilon^{4}+115\epsilon^{3}+318\epsilon^{2}+372\epsilon+128\right)

\displaystyle+2q_{0}^{4}\left(\epsilon^{3}+8\epsilon^{2}+19\epsilon+12\right)\biggr]

\displaystyle C_{3}^{Q^{3}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{q_{0}}{384\Lambda^{4}(\epsilon+2)^{2}(\epsilon+3)(\epsilon+5)(\epsilon+7)}\biggl[-2k_{0}^{3}q_{0}^{2}\left(\epsilon^{5}+18\epsilon^{4}+99\epsilon^{3}+175\epsilon^{2}-5\epsilon-164\right)

(4.78)

\displaystyle-k_{0}^{2}q_{0}^{3}\left(\epsilon^{5}+18\epsilon^{4}+67\epsilon^{3}-132\epsilon^{2}-874\epsilon-920\right)-k_{0}^{4}q_{0}\bigl(\epsilon^{5}+18\epsilon^{4}

\displaystyle+105\epsilon^{3}+238\epsilon^{2}+182\epsilon+8\bigr)+2k_{0}^{5}\left(\epsilon^{3}+8\epsilon^{2}+19\epsilon+12\right)

\displaystyle+2k_{0}q_{0}^{4}\left(16\epsilon^{3}+149\epsilon^{2}+419\epsilon+364\right)+2q_{0}^{5}\left(4\epsilon^{3}+35\epsilon^{2}+97\epsilon+84\right)\biggr]

\displaystyle C_{4}^{Q^{3}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

(4.79)

Notice that, since the coefficients are polynomials in
k_{0},p_{0},q_{0}
, we could easily replace:
p_{0}=-k_{0}-q_{0}
, since this part is independent on the choice of boundary conditions in the propagators.
We need to be much more careful instead in keeping tracks of
k_{0},p_{0},q_{0}
in the Master Integrals.

It is remarkable that the coefficient
C_{4}^{Q^{3}}
is exactly
0
in
d
-dimensions.

(4.83)

where
J_{1}^{MI},J_{2}^{MI},J_{3}^{MI}
are factorizable in a product of two massive tadpoles, whereas
J_{4}
is irreducible.

The coefficient
C_{4}^{Q^{3}}
is zero, and that hugely simplifies the computation since we just need the explicit expression for the other 3 MI appearing, which are just products of massive tadpoles, with masses
k_{0},q_{0},p_{0}
and are given by:

\displaystyle J_{1}^{MI}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\Gamma\left(1-\frac{d}{2}\right)^{2}}{(4\pi)^{d}}(-k_{0}^{2})^{\frac{d-2}{2}}(-p_{0}^{2})^{\frac{d-2}{2}}\ ,

(4.84)

\displaystyle J_{2}^{MI}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\Gamma\left(1-\frac{d}{2}\right)^{2}}{(4\pi)^{d}}(-k_{0}^{2})^{\frac{d-2}{2}}(-q_{0}^{2})^{\frac{d-2}{2}}\ ,

(4.85)

\displaystyle J_{3}^{MI}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\Gamma\left(1-\frac{d}{2}\right)^{2}}{(4\pi)^{d}}(-p_{0}^{2})^{\frac{d-2}{2}}(-q_{0}^{2})^{\frac{d-2}{2}}\ .

(4.86)

If
When we substitute the explicit expression for the MI, and we take the limit
\epsilon\to 0
, we encounter some square root terms of the type
\sqrt{-k_{0}^{2}}
, where we must be careful in taking the correct prescriptions, which are given by:

\displaystyle\sqrt{-k_{0}^{2}}=ik_{0}\ ,\qquad\sqrt{-q_{0}^{2}}=iq_{0}\ ,\qquad\sqrt{-p_{0}^{2}}=-ip_{0}\ .

(4.87)

Result

We can obtain the final expression by substituting the explicit expression for the MI and taking the limit
\epsilon\to 0
:

\displaystyle S^{Q^{3}}_{eff\ 5PN}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{G_{N}^{2}}{315}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk_{0}}{(2\pi)}\frac{dq_{0}}{(2\pi)}\biggl(k_{0}^{4}\left(-32p_{0}^{2}q_{0}^{2}+28p_{0}^{3}q_{0}+21p_{0}^{4}+74p_{0}q_{0}^{3}-21q_{0}^{4}\right)

(4.88)

\displaystyle+32k_{0}^{2}p_{0}^{3}q_{0}^{3}+2k_{0}^{3}p_{0}q_{0}^{3}(2p_{0}+23q_{0})+28k_{0}p_{0}^{4}q_{0}^{3}+21p_{0}^{4}q_{0}^{4}\biggr)Q_{ij}Q_{jk}Q_{ki}

If we move to time domain we get:

\displaystyle S^{Q^{3}}_{eff\ 5PN}=-\frac{G_{N}^{2}}{15}\int dt\biggl[\ddddot{Q}_{ij}\ddddot{Q}_{jk}Q_{ki}+\frac{4}{7}\dddot{Q}_{ij}\dddot{Q}_{jk}\ddot{Q}_{ki}\biggr]

(4.89)

This result agrees with Eq.(27) of
[
84
]
.

The corresponding contribution to the effective action is given by:

S_{EFF\ 5PN}^{Q^{3}2}=-i\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk_{0}}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dq_{0}}{2\pi}\mathcal{M}^{Q^{3}2}\ ,

(4.91)

where:

\mathcal{M}^{Q^{3}2}=\biggl(\mathcal{M}^{Q^{3}2}_{\sigma^{2}}+\mathcal{M}^{Q^{3}2}_{A^{2}}+\mathcal{M}^{Q^{3}2}_{\phi^{2}}+\mathcal{M}^{Q^{3}2}_{\sigma A}+\mathcal{M}^{Q^{3}2}_{\sigma\phi}+\mathcal{M}^{Q^{3}2}_{A\phi}\biggr)\ .

(4.92)

Once we substitute the Feynman rules, apply tensor contractions and tensor decomposition, it turns out that only
\mathcal{M}^{Q^{3}2}_{\sigma^{2}}
is non-vanishing, all the other diagrams give a zero result, and we get:

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{Q^{3}2}=Q_{ij}(k_{0})Q_{jk}(q_{0})Q_{ki}(p_{0})\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{Q^{3}2}

(4.93)

4.5.2
IBP decomposition

4.72
). The total amplitude can then be written in terms of 1 Master Integral:
